# Syllabus

This is a sample syllabus for an approximately sixteen-week semester. For WPI
students, Canvas and the official academic calendar remain the authoritative
sources for policies and deadlines. The sample is also intended to help other
instructors adapt the openly available notes and projects.

## Learning Outcomes

By the end of the course, students should be able to:

1. Implement and explain probabilistic navigation methods built on Bayesian,
   Kalman-style, and Monte Carlo estimation.
2. Develop sensor, propagation, and fusion models for a dynamic vehicle.
3. Evaluate a navigation system using accuracy, uncertainty, consistency, and
   computational-cost evidence.
4. Apply the same estimation ideas from local robotics problems through global
   inertial and GNSS navigation.

## Textbooks

The notes draw primarily from:

- *Probabilistic Robotics* by Thrun, Burgard, and Fox;
- *Robotics, Vision and Control* by Peter Corke;
- *Principles of GNSS, Inertial, and Multisensor Integrated Navigation Systems*
  by Paul Groves; and
- Roger Labbe's *Kalman and Bayesian Filters in Python*.

## Course Requirements

The course is project centered. Modules build on one another but remain
individually assessable. Each submission includes source code and a short
technical report that explains model choices, results, limitations, and the
evidence supporting the conclusions. Python is the supported language for course
examples and debugging support; students may use another language when they can
still meet the required deliverables.

## Grading Policy

The course follows the standard A--F scale. The exact deadline and any extension
policy are set by the official course offering. The sample module weights are:

- Module 1: Visual-Inertial Navigation -- 50%
  - Part A: Dead Reckoning and Sensor Characterization -- 25%
  - Part B: PnP Observation Model -- 25%
  - Part C: Nonlinear Navigation Filters -- 50%
- Module 2: Victoria Park FastSLAM -- 25%
- Module 3: INS/GNSS Integration -- 25%

An acceptable submission demonstrates a correct, documented implementation and
honest analysis. Higher ratings require clearer justification of state,
measurement, covariance, and validation choices. Code that runs is necessary;
it is not by itself evidence that the navigation model is correct.

| Letter grade | Percentage |
|---|---:|
| A | 90--100 |
| B | 80--89 |
| C | 70--79 |
| D | 60--69 |
| F | Below 60 |

## Course Schedule

The schedule is a suggested sequencing of the rendered book. It does not add
assessment requirements to the optional advanced chapters.

| Week | Topics | Suggested milestone |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | Course orientation; GNC; coordinate-frame and attitude conventions | |
| 2 | Linear algebra, probability, and scientific Python refresh | |
| 3 | Sensor taxonomy, motion models, IMU errors, and dead reckoning | Module 1A |
| 4 | Measurement models, data association, and PnP vision | |
| 5 | Camera-to-robot observation models and covariance | Module 1B |
| 6 | Bayes filtering and the Kalman-filter review | |
| 7 | EKF, error-state filtering, and consistency diagnostics | |
| 8 | UKF, information filters, and particle filters | Module 1C |
| 9 | Filter comparison, project integration, and implementation review | Module 1 |
| 10 | Mapping, landmark SLAM, and data association | |
| 11 | FastSLAM, visual navigation, and loop closure | Module 2 |
| 12 | Global frames, GNSS measurements, and IMU error models | |
| 13 | Curved-Earth INS/GNSS integration and observability | Module 3 |
| 14 | Timing, health monitoring, validation, and production software | |
| 15 | Optional advanced topics: smoothing, GNSS receiver-to-fusion, and resilient navigation | |
| 16 | Integration, review, and project completion | All module submissions |
